name: Native American Animism
line: Relate to land, animals and weather as kin.

quote.text: Mitákuye Oyás’iŋ: we are all related.
quote.source: Spoken at the close of prayers

quotes.text: Paying attention is a form of reciprocity with the living world.
The old Lakota was wise. He knew that man’s heart, away from nature, becomes hard.
Once in his life a man ought to concentrate his mind upon the remembered earth.

words.meaning: All my relations; we are all related
words.usage: Said at the end of a prayer. It includes people, animals, plants, stones and weather.
Also the name of a giving of thanks.
Not a thing but a quality that anything may carry.
Heard around the world from Standing Rock in 2016.
The earth addressed as an elder relative.

words.meaning: Extended family; the circle one lives in
words.usage: The basic unit of Lakota society, wider than a household.
A whole way of living, summed up as walking in beauty.
Everyday thanks.
A greeting and a blessing in one word.

words.meaning: Kinship; the way of being related
words.usage: Diné introduce themselves by their four clans before anything else.
The Navajo Nation’s name for itself.
The confederacy of six nations. "Iroquois" is an outsiders’ name.

words.meaning: The words that come before all else
words.usage: The Thanksgiving Address, spoken to open gatherings.
Everyday thanks.
One of the three principles of the Great Law, with power and a good mind.
Heard across the Great Lakes.
The common greeting.
The food that grows on water, at the centre of Anishinaabe life.
Life lived in balance with all relations.
Land as home and relative, not as property.
Anishinaabe women are its traditional keepers.

words.meaning: The force that causes mushrooms to push up from the earth overnight
words.usage: A word Robin Wall Kimmerer describes finding in an Anishinaabe ethnobotany.
The Cherokee Nation’s greeting.
Everyday thanks.

words.meaning: Working together for the good of the community
words.usage: A Cherokee value: everyone helps and no one is left out.
The v is a short "uh" sound.
Everyday thanks.
The common greeting.
From the Pacific Northwest coast.
From south-western Alaska.
A way of living that calls for another way.
In Haudenosaunee and Anishinaabe tellings the land was formed on a turtle’s back.
words.language: English, from several nations’ creation stories

practices.name: Morning thanks
practices.instructions: Step outside or stand at an open window before you do anything else. In your own words, and aloud if you can, give thanks in turn: to the people around you, the ground, the water, the plants that feed you, the animals, the trees, the birds, the wind, the sun. Be specific about what is actually here today. Finish by asking yourself what you can give back.
practices.why: The Haudenosaunee open gatherings with the Thanksgiving Address, greeting each part of the living world in order. That address is theirs. What anyone can learn from it is the habit of beginning with thanks.
variations: Read the published Thanksgiving Address once as a listener, not a performer.
Give thanks to one thing only, at length.
Do it with a child and let them choose the order.

practices.name: Sit spot
practices.instructions: Choose one place outdoors you can reach every day: a garden corner, a park bench, a doorstep. Go there, sit, and stay for twenty minutes without a phone. Notice what is growing, what is moving, what you can hear, how the light falls. Return to exactly the same place each day and see what you begin to recognise.
practices.why: This is a nature-awareness practice from outdoor education, not a ceremony. It is here because relationship with a place starts the way any relationship does: by turning up and paying attention.
variations: Go at a different hour and compare.
Sit in the rain.
Sketch a simple map of everything living within ten paces.

practices.name: Greet one tree
practices.instructions: Choose one tree on your way out of the door and greet it as you would a neighbour: look at it, say hello, notice what it is doing today, whether it is in bud, leaf or fruit, who is living in it. Do the same tree every day, so that you get to know it. A tree is a long-term neighbour, and it will be there after you.
practices.why: Robin Wall Kimmerer writes of the grammar of animacy in her language, in which a tree is a who and not an it. You do not need the language to try the habit of greeting.
variations: Touch the bark, if the tree allows.
Learn its name and tell someone.
Visit the same tree at night.

practices.name: Know today’s sky
practices.instructions: Look up and read the sky. What is the weather doing? Which way is the wind? Where is the sun, and where would the moon be? Is it waxing or waning? Look up the phase of the moon, and say it aloud: today it is a waxing crescent. Many peoples have lived by this reading. It makes you a person of the place.
practices.why: Knowledge of a place begins with attention to what is above it. Many Native nations keep calendars tied to moons and seasons, and these belong to the nations that keep them. Looking up is a way to begin to learn from them.
variations: Note the weather and sky in one line each day.
Learn the name of the season in your region, not the calendar.
Stay out for ten minutes until you notice a change.

practices.name: Trace your breakfast
practices.instructions: As you eat breakfast, trace each item back as far as you can: the oats or the bread, the fruit, the milk, the coffee or tea. Whose land grew it? Which water fed it? Who picked it and who carried it? Say a quiet thank you for each. It is a small way of seeing a meal as a web of relations.
practices.why: In the Native view relationships run through everything, including food. Tracing a breakfast makes a thing that seems ordinary into a long chain of care.
variations: Do it for one item only, very deeply.
Do it with a child, asking where it all came from.
Choose one local item and find out where it grew.

practices.name: Water first
practices.instructions: Pour a glass of water, hold it, and say thank you to the water. Mní wičhóni, water is life, is the call of the Lakota water protectors. Know where your own comes from. Drink the glass slowly. Then carry one thought into the day: how will I treat the water I use?
practices.why: For many Native nations water is a relative, not a resource. Mní wičhóni became the cry of Standing Rock. Drinking a glass with thanks is a small and honest way to join the thought.
variations: Find where your tap water comes from, by name.
Take your first glass outside.
Notice each time you use water today.

practices.name: Listen to the place
practices.instructions: Go outside, close your eyes, and count the separate sounds you can hear: near, middle, far. Name each one silently (wind, a bird, a car, water). Then open your eyes and find the source of one you could not place. Ask, without expecting an answer: who lives here, and what are they doing right now?
practices.why: Many Native traditions teach that knowledge of a place comes first from attention and relationship, long before anything is written about it.
variations: Do it at the same spot every day.
Draw a map of the sounds.
Do it at night.

practices.name: Learn one plant or animal by name
practices.instructions: Pick one plant, tree, bird or insect that lives where you live. Learn its common name. Then learn something about its life: what it eats, who eats it, when it flowers or arrives. If the Indigenous language of your area has a name for it and that name is shared publicly, learn that too.
practices.why: Robin Wall Kimmerer writes that learning the names of plants is the first step in ceasing to treat them as scenery. You do not ignore those you know by name.
variations: Follow one tree through the whole Onda.
Learn which plants near you are native and which arrived.
Learn the name of your watershed.

practices.name: Whose land is this?
practices.instructions: Find out whose land you are standing on. Use a free resource such as Native Land Digital, and look at the names of the nations whose homeland it is, and which of them are still here. Read one thing that they have published about themselves. An acknowledgment is a first lesson, not a last one. Ask what you can do next.
practices.why: The rule of this Onda is to name the nation. Learning whose land you are on is the beginning of a relationship, and it moves attention from the abstract to the particular.
variations: Look up the treaty or the lack of one.
Find a Native-run organisation in your region and read their page.
Tell one person what you learned.

practices.name: Harvest with honour
practices.instructions: If something is growing near you that is safe and fine to pick, berries, mint, herbs, windfall apples, pick it as Robin Wall Kimmerer describes the Honorable Harvest: ask first, in your mind; never take the first or the last; take only what you need; use what you take; share some; and say thank you. If there is nothing to pick, buy something from a local grower and do the same.
practices.why: Kimmerer describes the Honorable Harvest as a code of Native reciprocity, found in many nations. It is a modern way to treat everything you take as a gift.
variations: Harvest nothing; just ask what you could take and leave it.
Share what you pick within the hour.
Learn one safe plant first from a field guide.

practices.name: Give something back
practices.instructions: Give something back to the place you live: pick up litter, water a tree, pull an invasive weed, plant a seed, clean a drain so the rain can get through. Make it a small, concrete thing. Notice how different your walk home feels when you have left it a bit better. It is the other half of taking.
practices.why: Reciprocity is the heart of this Onda: take only what you need, give before you take. A small act of giving back keeps the account open and honest.
variations: Give back something to a place you love.
Do it with a child and explain why.
Plant a native seed in a pot.

practices.name: Read a Native author
practices.instructions: Read a page, a poem or a short essay by a Native writer today, and let it be the voice. Joy Harjo, Robin Wall Kimmerer, N. Scott Momaday, Louise Erdrich and many others are easy to find. Note the nation they come from. Read slowly, as a guest, and let the words say what they say without turning them into advice for you.
practices.why: The rule of this Onda is to learn from Native voices and name their nations. Reading is one way to listen without taking anything that is not offered.
variations: Read a poem aloud.
Read a short story by a Native writer.
Follow a Native writer and share one post with a friend.

practices.name: Evening thanks
practices.instructions: Before sleep, recall what fed, sheltered and carried you today, and say thank you. Then name one thing you took and one thing you gave. If the taking was larger, decide what you will give tomorrow.
practices.why: Gratitude in this sense is not a mood. It is the acknowledgement of a debt, and it leads to reciprocity.
variations: Say it at the table before the evening meal.
Write a line of thanks to someone and send it.
Leave water out for birds.

practices.name: Leave water for the birds
practices.instructions: Put out a shallow dish of fresh water for the birds and insects. Choose a spot with a clear view and some cover, so they feel safe. Check it each day and clean it. Watch who comes. This is a small way to give back to the creatures who share your place, and it costs only a saucer.
practices.why: Sharing water with other beings is a simple act of reciprocity. It also trains the eye to see who lives alongside you.
variations: Add a few stones for bees to stand on.
Keep a note of each visitor.
Help a neighbour set up their own.

practices.name: Tell a story of this place
practices.instructions: Sit with someone and tell a true story about the place where you live: what happened on this street, what the land was before it, a time the river rose. If you do not know one, find one at the library or from an older neighbour, and tell it tomorrow. Stories are how a place is remembered.
practices.why: Many Native nations hold that stories are bound to places, and that a place is known through its stories. Learn a story from the people it belongs to, and then pass on what they allow you to share.
variations: Ask an older neighbour for a story.
Tell it to a child.
Write it down and keep it.

practices.name: Under the night sky
practices.instructions: Go outside after dark and look up for ten minutes without a phone. See what is there: the moon, planets, stars, the Milky Way if the sky is clear. Let your eyes adjust slowly. Think of all the people who have looked at this same sky from this same land. Notice what it does to your sense of size.
practices.why: Many Native nations have deep knowledge and stories of the night sky, which belong to them. A quiet look upward is a good first step toward listening to those who know it.
variations: Lie on a blanket.
Learn one star or planet by name.
Go with someone and take turns pointing.

practices.name: Eat what grows near you
practices.instructions: Cook a meal built around what grows in your region: local vegetables, beans, squash, corn, berries or greens. If you can, buy from a local grower or a Native-owned business. As you eat, say where each thing comes from and who may have grown it. Make it a meal that could not be made anywhere else.
practices.why: The Three Sisters, corn, beans and squash, grown together, are a famous Native planting, and many nations have their own foods of the place. Eating local is eating in relationship.
variations: Make a pot of Three Sisters stew.
Visit a farmers’ market first.
Share the meal with a neighbour.

practices.name: Ask an elder about their place
practices.instructions: Call or visit an older person you know, and ask about the place they grew up: what the land was like, who lived there, what has changed. Listen, ask one follow-up, and thank them. Elders are the memory of a place. This works with a grandparent, an older neighbour or someone from a community group.
practices.why: The rule of this Onda is to listen before you speak, especially to elders. Their memories are the oldest record of a place, and few people ask.
variations: Write down one thing they said.
Record a short voice note with permission.
Ask them where they feel at home.

practices.name: A morning with no roof
practices.instructions: On a free morning, spend two hours outdoors, in a park, a field, a wood or a garden, with no screen. Bring water and a notebook. Walk for a while, sit for a while, and notice. Say hello to what you meet. When you leave, thank the place out loud. You will see how much of the world you pass without looking.
practices.why: Time on the land is the basic practice of this Onda, and it is open to everyone. Two unhurried hours do more to build a relationship with a place than many short visits.
variations: Go with a friend and say little.
Go with a child and follow their pace.
Go back to the same place the next week.

practices.name: Follow the water
practices.instructions: Start at a drain or a gutter after rain, and follow the water downhill. Where does it go? Which stream, which river, which sea? Walk it as far as you can, and look at what lives along it. Find the name of your watershed, and its other names if there are any. It is a pleasant detective walk and a way to learn where you live.
practices.why: A watershed is the land that drains to one river. Many Native nations know their watersheds as homelands. Following the water teaches the geography of care.
variations: Do it with a map.
Do it after rain.
Pick up any litter along the way.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of Braiding Sweetgrass
immersePlan.text: Read one chapter of Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book, a botanist’s writing on reciprocity and the language of animacy. Notice the plant she is writing about, and then look for it near you.

immersePlan.name: Read the Thanksgiving Address as a listener
immersePlan.text: Read the Haudenosaunee Thanksgiving Address, shared publicly in Mohawk and English. Read it slowly as a listener, not a performer. Notice the order in which the living world is greeted.

immersePlan.name: Read a section of Rainy Mountain
immersePlan.text: Read a few pages of N. Scott Momaday’s book, in which Kiowa story, history and memory are told in three voices. Notice how place and story are knotted.

immersePlan.name: Watch an episode of Reservation Dogs
immersePlan.text: Watch one episode of the series written, directed and acted by Indigenous people, about four teenagers in rural Oklahoma. Notice what is funny, and who is allowed to be funny about it.

immersePlan.name: Watch Gather
immersePlan.text: Watch the documentary about Native communities reclaiming food: bison, salmon, wild plants. Notice how food, language and land are tied together.

immersePlan.name: Watch Smoke Signals
immersePlan.text: Watch the road film from the Coeur d’Alene reservation, a landmark of Native cinema. Notice the dry humour and the way it handles a father and a son.

immersePlan.name: Listen to All My Relations
immersePlan.text: Play an episode of the podcast about relationships to land, to creatures and to one another, hosted by Matika Wilbur and Adrienne Keene. Listen while you wash up or walk.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Canyon Trilogy
immersePlan.text: Play R. Carlos Nakai’s solo Native American flute album. Sit by a window, close your eyes, and let the breath in each note carry you for ten minutes.

immersePlan.name: Hear Joanne Shenandoah’s songs
immersePlan.text: Play a track of Haudenosaunee women’s songs by Joanne Shenandoah. Listen once through, then think of one woman who shaped you.

immersePlan.name: Look at I See Red: Target
immersePlan.text: Look at Jaune Quick-to-See Smith’s painting, which answers centuries of stereotypes. Notice what she has put in the target and what she has refused.

immersePlan.name: Look at Maria Martinez’s pottery
immersePlan.text: Look at the matte and polished black pottery of Maria Martinez of San Ildefonso Pueblo, made with her husband Julian. Notice the tension between shine and matte.

immersePlan.name: Look at Diné weaving
immersePlan.text: Look at Navajo weavings, and look at how a weaver closes the border, and ask why. Choose one pattern and say what it does to your eye.

immersePlan.name: Make a Three Sisters stew
immersePlan.text: Simmer corn, beans and squash together, the three plants many nations grow together. Notice how each one helps the other: the corn holds the bean, the squash shades the ground. Eat it slowly and thank each sister.

immersePlan.name: Cook manoomin
immersePlan.text: Cook wild rice, buying from a Native harvester in the Great Lakes region if you can. Rinse it, simmer until it blooms, and taste the nutty grain. Eat it plain first.

immersePlan.name: Eat berries with thanks
immersePlan.text: Eat a handful of whatever berries are in season, fresh. Slow down and taste each one. Say thank you to the plant before you eat.

immersePlan.name: Drink water knowing its source
immersePlan.text: Look up where your tap water comes from, then drink a glass of it slowly, naming that source aloud. Mní wičhóni: water is life.

immersePlan.name: Steep wild mint tea
immersePlan.text: Steep fresh or dried mint leaves in hot water for a few minutes. It is a common, widely shared drink. Notice the scent as it steeps, and drink it slowly.

immersePlan.name: Taste maple water
immersePlan.text: If you can find maple water, the sap before boiling, drink a glass cold. Anishinaabe families have tapped maples each spring for generations. If not, taste a spoonful of maple syrup and think of the work.

immersePlan.name: Thank the food before you eat
immersePlan.text: Before one meal today, say in your own words where the food came from, and thank it. Keep it short, true and specific, and then eat.

immersePlan.name: Name the nation whose land you are on
immersePlan.text: Look up which Native nation’s homeland you are in. Say its name aloud, and learn how it is pronounced. An acknowledgment is a first lesson, not a last one.

immersePlan.name: Practise the Honorable Harvest
immersePlan.text: Take only what you need, never the first or last, use what you take, share some, and give thanks. Apply it to one thing today: a snack, a flower, a glass of water.

immersePlan.name: Play a little of Never Alone
immersePlan.text: Play a level of the game made with nearly forty Alaska Native elders and storytellers, in which a girl and an arctic fox travel together. If you do not have it, watch a short video of it.

immersePlan.name: Play When Rivers Were Trails
immersePlan.text: Play the game in which you are an Anishinaabe person displaced from Minnesota in the 1890s. It is free and made with Native communities. Notice the choices it asks of you.

immersePlan.name: Throw and catch a ball with a friend
immersePlan.text: Lacrosse is the Creator’s Game of the Haudenosaunee, played as medicine as well as sport. Do a small version: throw and catch a ball with a friend for ten minutes, and say thank you at the end.

immersePlan.name: Mark Indigenous Peoples’ Day
immersePlan.text: Indigenous Peoples’ Day falls on the second Monday of October in the US. Find a talk, a market or an exhibition by Indigenous people, and go or watch. Buy something from a Native maker.

immersePlan.name: Find a Native heritage event
immersePlan.text: November is Native American Heritage Month in the US. Look up one museum, library or tribal cultural centre programme, and attend or watch one thing online.

immersePlan.name: Look at Cahokia Mounds
immersePlan.text: Look up Cahokia Mounds, the remains of the largest city north of Mexico before 1500. Find a picture of Monks Mound, and imagine the city on the river. Notice who is telling the story.

immersePlan.name: Say Mitákuye Oyás’iŋ
immersePlan.text: Mitákuye Oyás’iŋ is Lakota for all my relations. Say it aloud as you look at someone or something you are in relationship with: a person, a tree, a river. Learn how it is pronounced.

immersePlan.name: Say Miigwech
immersePlan.text: Miigwech is Anishinaabemowin for thank you. Say it, with care for its pronunciation, to someone today who has given you something, even a small thing, and look at them as you say it.

immersePlan.name: Ask what mino-bimaadiziwin looks like
immersePlan.text: Mino-bimaadiziwin is Anishinaabe for the good life, living well. Ask: what would a good life look like for me, my family, the land? Write three lines in answer, and share one with someone.

rules.why: The first rule of what Kimmerer calls the Honorable Harvest, a set of principles shared in different forms by many peoples. Pick one thing today and take less of it.

rules.text: Say thank you aloud to what feeds you
rules.why: Speaking it makes the relationship real to you, and a spoken thanks is hard to fake.

rules.text: Do not imitate sacred ceremonies you were not invited to
rules.why: Sweat lodges, pipe ceremonies, vision quests and sun dances belong to specific nations and are led by people with the right to lead them. Until 1978 many were restricted by United States law. They are not included here.

rules.text: Listen before you speak, especially to elders
rules.why: In most Native communities knowledge is earned by listening and by relationship, not requested on demand.
There is no single Native American culture. Say Diné, Lakota, Haudenosaunee, Cherokee, and say which you mean.
Reciprocity: leave a place better than you found it, and support Native communities with more than interest.

read.title: The Way to Rainy Mountain

read.why: Kiowa story, history and memory told in three voices.

read.title: Ceremony

read.title: Land of the Spotted Eagle

read.why: Lakota life and thought described from the inside.

read.title: An American Sunrise
read.creator: Joy Harjo (Muscogee Nation)
read.why: Poems on return to the land her people were removed from.

read.title: The Heartbeat of Wounded Knee
read.creator: David Treuer (Leech Lake Ojibwe)
read.why: Native America from 1890 to the present: not an ending but a continuing.

read.title: All Our Relations
read.creator: Winona LaDuke (White Earth Ojibwe)
read.why: Native struggles for land and life, nation by nation.

watch.creator: Sterlin Harjo (Seminole and Muscogee) and Taika Waititi
watch.why: Four teenagers in rural Oklahoma. Written, directed and acted by Indigenous people.

watch.why: Native communities reclaiming food: bison, salmon, wild plants.

watch.title: Rumble: The Indians Who Rocked the World

watch.title: Fancy Dance

watch.why: An aunt and niece head for a powwow while searching for a missing woman.

listen.title: All My Relations
listen.creator: Matika Wilbur (Swinomish and Tulalip) and Adrienne Keene (Cherokee Nation)
listen.why: A podcast on relationships to land, to creatures and to one another.

listen.title: Toasted Sister Podcast
listen.creator: Andi Murphy (Diné)
listen.why: Conversations about Native food and the people bringing it back.

listen.title: Powwow singing
listen.creator: Any Native-run recording or a public powwow
listen.why: Listen for the lead singer’s call and the drum group’s answer.

art.title: I See Red: Target
art.creator: Jaune Quick-to-See Smith (Salish and Kootenai)
art.why: A painting that answers centuries of stereotypes.

art.title: Black-on-black pottery
art.creator: Maria Martinez (San Ildefonso Pueblo)
art.why: Matte and polished black, made with her husband Julian.

art.title: Diné weaving
art.creator: Navajo weavers
art.why: Look at how a weaver closes the border, and ask why.

art.title: Paintings of T. C. Cannon
art.creator: T. C. Cannon (Kiowa and Caddo)
art.why: Bright, ironic portraits of Native people in the modern world.

art.title: National Museum of the American Indian
art.creator: Washington and New York
art.why: A Smithsonian museum developed with Native communities. Much of the collection is online.

eat.title: Three Sisters stew
eat.creator: Corn, beans and squash
eat.why: Grown together by the Haudenosaunee and many other nations: each plant helps the other two.

eat.title: Wild rice
eat.creator: Manoomin, hand-harvested
eat.why: Buy it from Native harvesters in the Great Lakes region.

eat.title: Seasonal berries
eat.creator: Whatever grows near you
eat.why: Eaten fresh, with thanks to the plant.

eat.title: A recipe from The Sioux Chef’s Indigenous Kitchen
eat.creator: Sean Sherman (Oglala Lakota)
eat.why: Indigenous ingredients without wheat flour, dairy or refined sugar.

drink.title: Water
drink.creator: Mní wičhóni
drink.why: Drink it knowing where it comes from. Find the source of your tap water.

drink.title: Maple water
drink.creator: Sap, before boiling
drink.why: Anishinaabe families have tapped maples each spring for generations.

customs.title: Offer thanks before eating
customs.creator: In your own words
customs.why: Name where the food came from.

customs.title: Honor elders first
customs.creator: Serve them before yourself
customs.why: At most Native gatherings elders eat first and speak when they choose.

customs.title: Learn whose land you are on
customs.creator: Then ask what you can do
customs.why: An acknowledgment is a first lesson, not a last one. Native Land Digital maps territories, languages and treaties.

customs.title: The Honorable Harvest
customs.creator: As described by Robin Wall Kimmerer
customs.why: Ask permission. Never take the first or the last. Take only what you need. Use everything. Give thanks. Give a gift in return.

customs.title: Visit a public powwow as a guest
customs.creator: Where the public is welcome
customs.why: Stand when asked, ask before photographing, never touch regalia, and listen to the announcer.

customs.title: Buy from Native makers
customs.creator: Directly where possible
customs.why: In the United States it is illegal to sell work as Native-made when it is not.

games.title: Never Alone (Kisima Ingitchuna)
games.creator: Video game · Upper One Games with the Iñupiat community
games.why: Made with nearly forty Alaska Native elders and storytellers. A girl and an arctic fox travel through a traditional story, with short films of people explaining the world behind it.

games.title: When Rivers Were Trails
games.creator: Video game · Indian Land Tenure Foundation and Michigan State University
games.why: You play an Anishinaabe person displaced from Minnesota in the 1890s. Written by more than twenty Indigenous writers and free to download.

games.title: Lacrosse
games.creator: Field game · Haudenosaunee and other nations
games.why: Known to the Haudenosaunee as the Creator’s Game and played as medicine as well as sport. Watch a match or learn its history from Haudenosaunee sources.

games.title: Hand game
games.creator: Guessing game · many nations
games.why: Two teams, hidden bones and a great deal of singing. Played at public gatherings across the West. Watch first, and join only if invited.

festivals.title: Gathering of Nations
festivals.creator: Late April, Albuquerque, New Mexico
festivals.why: One of the largest powwows in North America, with dancers and drum groups from hundreds of nations. It is open to the public.

festivals.title: Indigenous Peoples’ Day
festivals.creator: Second Monday of October, USA
festivals.why: A day of public events, talks and markets in many cities. A good day to learn whose land you live on.

festivals.title: Native American Heritage Month
festivals.creator: November, USA
festivals.why: Museums, libraries and tribal cultural centres run programmes all month. Look for events led by Native presenters.

festivals.title: Local powwows
festivals.creator: Mostly spring to autumn
festivals.why: Many are open to visitors. Stand for the grand entry, ask before taking photographs and follow the announcer’s guidance.

places.title: National Museum of the American Indian
places.creator: Washington, DC, and New York, USA
places.why: A Smithsonian museum whose exhibitions are made with Native communities and speak in their own voices.

places.title: Cahokia Mounds
places.creator: Collinsville, Illinois, USA
places.why: The remains of the largest city north of Mexico before 1500, with a great earthen mound you can climb. A World Heritage Site.

places.title: Chaco Culture National Historical Park
places.creator: New Mexico, USA
places.why: Great houses aligned to the sun and moon, built by ancestral Pueblo people. It remains sacred to their descendants, so walk gently.

places.title: Taos Pueblo
places.creator: New Mexico, USA
places.why: A living community in adobe buildings that have been lived in for about a thousand years. Visitors are welcome on most days; check closures and follow the rules on photographs.

places.title: Heard Museum
places.creator: Phoenix, Arizona, USA
places.why: A museum of Native art old and new, with a frank exhibition on the boarding school era.

ethics.title: Reciprocity
ethics.text: What you take, you answer with a gift. The relationship between people and land runs both ways, and gratitude is how it begins.
ethics.practice: Match one thing you take today with one thing you give.

ethics.title: Kinship with all beings
ethics.text: Other species are spoken of as relatives, elders and teachers. Relatives are owed respect, and are not resources.
ethics.practice: Address one non-human being today as "you", not "it".

ethics.title: Respect cultural protocols
ethics.text: Knowledge belongs to peoples and is shared on their terms. Some of it is not shared at all, and that is to be respected.
ethics.practice: When you learn something from a Native source, note who it came from and what they asked of the listener.

ethics.title: Responsibility before rights
ethics.text: Many Native legal and ethical traditions begin from what one owes: to family, to nation, to land, to those not yet born.
ethics.practice: List your responsibilities to the place you live.

ethics.title: The Honorable Harvest
ethics.text: Take only what is given, only what you need, and in a way that does no harm. Share it. Be grateful. Sustain the ones who sustain you.
ethics.practice: Apply it to one purchase today.

ethics.title: Thinking of those to come
ethics.text: Haudenosaunee teaching asks leaders to consider the effect of each decision on the seventh generation.
ethics.practice: Choose once today for someone who is not born yet.

philosophy.title: Everything is alive and related
philosophy.text: Many Native languages treat rivers, mountains and animals grammatically as persons. The world is made of relatives, not objects.
philosophy.practice: For one hour, think of the things around you as "who".

philosophy.title: Place as teacher
philosophy.text: Vine Deloria Jr. argued that Native thought begins from particular places and what they teach, where Western thought begins from time and history.
philosophy.practice: Ask what the place you live would have you learn.

philosophy.title: Seven generations
philosophy.text: A decision is weighed by what it does to people seven generations on, and by what the seven before would say of it.
philosophy.practice: Before a decision, picture a great-grandchild watching.

philosophy.title: Gratitude as a way of seeing
philosophy.text: Giving thanks to each part of the world, in order, is a way of counting what is present and noticing what is missing.
philosophy.practice: Give thanks today to something you have never thanked.

philosophy.title: The gift
philosophy.text: Kimmerer: a gift creates ongoing relationship. Treating the world as gift, not commodity, changes what you may do with it.
philosophy.practice: Receive one thing today as a gift and see what it asks in return.

philosophy.title: Knowledge is relationship
philosophy.text: To know a plant or a river is to have duties toward it. Knowing is not standing apart and observing.
philosophy.practice: Learn one thing about a neighbour species, and do one thing for it.

philosophy.title: Walking in beauty
philosophy.text: The Diné ideal of hózhó: a life in balance with what is before, behind, above, below and around you.
philosophy.practice: Notice where you are out of balance, and make one correction.

philosophy.title: Story carries law
philosophy.text: Stories told in the right season hold instruction about how to live. They belong to their tellers.
philosophy.practice: Recall a story you were told as a child that taught you how to behave.

philosophy.title: Language holds a world
philosophy.text: Each of the many Native languages holds knowledge that exists nowhere else. When one goes silent, so does that knowledge.
philosophy.practice: Learn to say thank you in the language of the land you live on.

philosophy.title: Survivance
philosophy.text: The Anishinaabe writer Gerald Vizenor’s word: more than survival. An active presence, a refusal of tragedy and victimhood.
philosophy.practice: Read or listen to one living Native voice today.

journal: What did you thank today, and what did you take?
What did the land teach you?
Who or what did you treat as kin?
What will you give back?
What did you notice at your sit spot that you had missed before?
Whose land do you live on, and what do you know about them now?
What did you learn the name of?
Where does your water come from?
What did you take more of than you needed?
What did you eat today, and what did it cost the world?
Who are your elders, and when did you last listen to them?
What have you inherited that you did not earn?
What will those seven generations on think of today?
What changed outside since yesterday?
Which living thing near you do you know best? Least?
What did you assume about Native people that you now doubt?
What gift did you receive today?
What responsibility have you been avoiding?
What did you hear when you stopped talking?
What is the oldest living thing you saw today?
Where were you a guest today, and did you behave like one?
What story was told to you about this land? Who told it, and who was left out?
What would the plant you learned say about you?
What did you want to take home that was not yours?
How did the weather shape your day?
What did a Native author teach you this week?
What do you owe the place where you were born?
What can you do, beyond acknowledging?
What season is it really, where you are?
To whom are you related?
reflect: How has your sense of kinship with land and other beings changed?
Which practice changed you the most, and why?
Where did you resist, and what was the resistance protecting?
What do you now know about the people whose land you live on, and what will you do with it?
What have you given back, and what will you keep giving?
What did you learn about the limits of what is yours to take?

intro: This Onda is an invitation to practice one idea held, in many different forms, by the Indigenous peoples of North America: that land, water, plants, animals and weather are relatives, and that a good life is lived in reciprocity with them.

First, an honest note about the name. There is no single "Native American" religion or philosophy. There are 574 federally recognised tribal nations in the United States alone, hundreds more First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities in Canada, and well over a hundred distinct languages still spoken. A Diné sheep herder in Arizona, a Tlingit fisher in Alaska and a Haudenosaunee farmer in New York inherit different stories, laws and ceremonies. "Animism" is not their word either. It was coined by a Victorian anthropologist and long used to rank these traditions as primitive. It is kept here only because it points at something real: a world understood as full of persons, only some of whom are human.

What can be said in common is said best by Native writers themselves. The Lakota close prayers with mitákuye oyás’iŋ, all my relations. The Haudenosaunee open gatherings with the Thanksgiving Address, which greets the people, the earth, the waters, the fish, the plants, the animals, the trees, the birds, the winds, the sun, moon and stars in turn, ending each greeting: now our minds are one. The Diné speak of hózhó, a life walked in balance and beauty. The Potawatomi botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer describes a "grammar of animacy" in which a bay or a maple is not an it but a who, and an ethic, the Honorable Harvest, for taking from the world without damaging it.

These are living traditions that survived a determined attempt to end them. From the 1880s ceremonies were banned under United States regulations, and for generations children were taken to boarding schools designed to remove their languages and beliefs. Full legal protection for Native religious practice came only in 1978. That history is why Native communities guard their ceremonies, and why outsiders are asked not to imitate them.

So this Onda contains no ceremonies. There is no smudging, no sweat lodge, no pipe, no vision quest. It contains only what Native authors and nations have offered publicly, and what any guest can do: give thanks in your own words, learn the names of your non-human neighbours, find out whose land you live on, read and listen to Native people, take less and give something back.

Treat it as a beginning in being a better relative and a better guest. The content has been written with care from published Indigenous sources, but it has not yet been reviewed by Indigenous advisers, and it should be before this Onda is released.

figures.name: The Peacemaker and Hiawatha
figures.bio: By Haudenosaunee tradition they united five warring nations under the Great Law of Peace.

figures.name: Po’pay
figures.bio: Religious leader from Ohkay Owingeh who organised the Pueblo Revolt of 1680.

figures.name: Sequoyah
figures.bio: Cherokee creator of the Cherokee syllabary, completed in 1821.

figures.name: Black Elk (Heȟáka Sápa)
figures.bio: Oglala Lakota holy man whose account of his visions has been read around the world.

figures.name: Luther Standing Bear
figures.bio: Oglala Lakota author, actor and advocate. Among the first students at Carlisle.

figures.name: Zitkála-Šá
figures.bio: Yankton Dakota writer, musician and campaigner for citizenship and religious freedom.

figures.name: Ella Cara Deloria
figures.bio: Yankton Dakota linguist and novelist who recorded Dakota and Lakota language and kinship.

figures.name: Vine Deloria Jr.
figures.bio: Standing Rock Sioux lawyer, historian and philosopher. Author of God Is Red.

figures.name: Oren Lyons
figures.bio: Faithkeeper of the Onondaga Nation and a voice for Indigenous peoples at the United Nations.

figures.name: Wilma Mankiller
figures.bio: Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation from 1985 to 1995, the first woman in that office.

figures.name: Joy Harjo
figures.bio: Muscogee poet and musician. United States Poet Laureate from 2019 to 2022.

figures.name: Robin Wall Kimmerer
figures.bio: Citizen Potawatomi botanist and author of Braiding Sweetgrass.

history.detail: Nations’ own histories place them on their lands from the beginning. Fossil footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, have been dated to more than 21,000 years ago.

Five nations join under the Great Law of Peace. Tradition and scholarship offer dates from the twelfth to the fifteenth century. It is among the oldest continuing participatory governments in the world.
Pueblo peoples of the Rio Grande, coordinated by Po’pay, drive Spanish colonists out for twelve years after decades of forced labour and suppression of their religion.
Within a few years most Cherokee can read and write their language. A newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix, follows in 1828.
The Indian Removal Act forces the nations of the south-east west of the Mississippi. Thousands of Cherokee die on the Trail of Tears in 1838–39.

history.what: The Long Walk of the Diné
history.detail: The Navajo are marched to internment at Bosque Redondo. A treaty in 1868 allows them to return to part of their homeland.
The first of the federal off-reservation boarding schools, founded on the motto of removing the Indian to save the man. Hundreds of such schools operated into the twentieth century.
The Code of Indian Offenses bans dances, feasts and the practices of medicine people. The Sun Dance and other ceremonies continue in secret.
United States cavalry kill some 250 to 300 Lakota, many of them women and children, on 29 December.
Native people born in the United States are declared citizens. Several states deny them the vote for decades more.
Indians of All Tribes hold the island for nineteen months. The Red Power movement puts self-determination on the national agenda.

history.what: The American Indian Religious Freedom Act
history.detail: Federal law finally protects the right to believe, express and exercise traditional religions. The Indian Child Welfare Act passes the same year.

history.what: NAGPRA and the Native American Languages Act
history.detail: Museums must return ancestors’ remains and sacred objects. Federal policy turns to preserving languages it once punished.

history.what: The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
history.detail: Adopted by the General Assembly. The United States endorses it in 2010.
Thousands gather with the Standing Rock Sioux to oppose an oil pipeline under the Missouri River. Their phrase, water is life, travels worldwide.
Deb Haaland of Laguna Pueblo becomes Secretary of the Interior and opens a federal investigation into the boarding schools.

concepts.text: Everything exists in relationship, and persons are not only human.
concepts.detail: This is less a belief than a way of speaking and behaving. If the river is a relative, certain things cannot be done to it.
The human role is not master or steward so much as one participant with duties. Kimmerer asks: what can we give in return for the gifts of the earth?

concepts.text: Guidelines for taking from the living world.
concepts.detail: Know the ways of the ones who take care of you. Ask permission and abide by the answer. Never take the first or the last. Take only what you need and only what is given. Never take more than half. Use it respectfully, share, give thanks, and give a gift in return.

concepts.text: Languages that address the living world as persons.
concepts.detail: In Potawatomi, as Kimmerer describes it, most of the world is spoken of with the grammar used for family. English makes it an "it".

concepts.text: Law, ethics and identity come from particular places.
concepts.detail: Sacred sites are not interchangeable. This is why land return and site protection are religious questions as well as political ones.

concepts.text: Decisions are weighed by their effect on descendants.
concepts.detail: A principle of Haudenosaunee governance, now widely quoted, and often quoted loosely.
They are governments that predate the United States and hold treaties with it. Culture, land and self-government cannot be separated.

concepts.text: Knowledge carried by speech and memory.
concepts.detail: Stories are told by particular people at particular times of year, and some are not for outsiders. Being written down is not the measure of being true.

concepts.text: The right way to ask, receive and share.
concepts.detail: Who may tell a story, sing a song or lead a ceremony is a matter of law within each nation. Respecting protocol is the guest’s first duty.

concepts.text: Taking sacred or identifying things without permission.
concepts.detail: Headdresses as costume, sweat lodges for sale, invented "spirit animals". The harm is real: people have died in imitation ceremonies, and communities see what is most sacred to them turned into product.

facts.text: There are 574 federally recognised tribal nations in the United States.

The famous "Chief Seattle speech" quoted on posters, with its line about the earth not belonging to man, was written by a screenwriter in 1971. Seattle’s actual 1854 speech survives only in a much later reconstruction.
Corn, beans and squash planted together support one another: corn gives the beans a pole, beans fix nitrogen, and squash leaves shade out weeds.
The words squash, moose, raccoon, skunk and pecan all come into English from Algonquian languages.
Many Native religious ceremonies were restricted by United States regulations from 1883. The American Indian Religious Freedom Act passed in 1978.
Diné Bizaad, the Navajo language, was used by Navajo Code Talkers for a military code in the Second World War that was never broken.
The Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 makes it illegal in the United States to market goods as Native-made when they are not.
In Braiding Sweetgrass (2013) Robin Wall Kimmerer writes that nine first-language speakers of Potawatomi remained. Their language is now taught again by the Potawatomi nations.

glossary.meaning: A sovereign people with its own government, law and territory. Preferred to "tribe" by many.
Having a government-to-government relationship with the United States.
The clothing worn for dance and ceremony. Never a "costume".
A gathering for dance, song and community. Many are open to the public.
A person recognised by their community for knowledge and conduct, not only for age.
A statement naming the peoples of the land where one stands.

sensitivity.note: There is no single Native American tradition. This Onda draws only on what Native authors and nations have shared publicly, names the nation each idea comes from, and includes no ceremonies. You are a guest: give thanks in your own words, learn whose land you are on, and give something back.
requiredCaveats: Do not perform or imitate smudging, sweat lodges, pipe ceremonies, vision quests, sun dances or any other ceremony. They belong to specific nations.
Do not wear regalia or headdresses, and do not claim a "spirit animal".
Pronunciations are approximate. Learn words from speakers and from nations’ own language programmes.
"Animism" is an outsiders’ term with a colonial history. It is used here as a pointer, not a description any nation chose.
This content has not yet been reviewed by Indigenous advisers. It must be before release.
